title: Module 6: Acoustic Interfaces, Reflection and Transmission

questions.stem: Which statement best defines an ultrasound echo?
questions.explanation: An echo is the portion of sound that is reflected back to the transducer.

questions.stem: An acoustic interface is formed where:
questions.explanation: An interface is the boundary where two different media meet.

questions.stem: Which interaction provides the returning information used to form a pulse-echo ultrasound image?
questions.explanation: Pulse-echo imaging is built from reflected sound; echo strength reflects the intensity of the reflected wave.

questions.stem: A stronger returning echo is generally displayed as:
questions.explanation: Stronger echoes are displayed brighter on the grayscale image.

questions.stem: Transmission occurs when ultrasound:
options: Travels back along its original path
questions.explanation: Transmission is the portion of sound that continues into the next medium.

questions.stem: The amount of sound reflected at an interface is determined primarily by:
questions.explanation: The greater the impedance mismatch, the greater the reflection.

questions.stem: The direction of reflected sound is determined primarily by:
questions.explanation: Amount of reflection depends on impedance; direction depends on the incidence angle.

questions.stem: When a sound beam strikes an interface perpendicularly, the angle of incidence measured from the normal is:
questions.explanation: The beam travels along the normal, so the incidence angle is 0°.

questions.stem: At perpendicular incidence, reflected sound travels:
questions.explanation: The echo returns along the same path toward the transducer.

questions.stem: Which condition produces the strongest returning echo from a smooth interface?
questions.explanation: Smooth (specular) interfaces return the strongest echo at perpendicular incidence. The diaphragm is an example.

questions.stem: Oblique incidence occurs when the ultrasound beam strikes an interface:
options: At an angle other than 0° from the normal
questions.explanation: Any angle other than 0° from the normal is oblique.

questions.stem: For oblique incidence, the angle of reflection is:
questions.explanation: Angle of reflection = angle of incidence.

questions.stem: A smooth interface may appear weak or absent when:
options: The two media have identical densities
questions.explanation: At oblique incidence the reflected beam can miss the transducer.

questions.stem: Which action can improve visualization of a smooth reflector that appears weak because of oblique incidence?
questions.explanation: Probe angulation or repositioning can restore perpendicular incidence.

questions.stem: Which equation defines acoustic impedance?
questions.explanation: Impedance is the product of density and propagation speed.

questions.stem: Acoustic impedance depends on:
questions.explanation: Z = ρc.

questions.stem: The unit used for acoustic impedance is:
questions.explanation: Impedance is measured in Rayls or MRayls.

questions.stem: If density increases while propagation speed remains constant, acoustic impedance will:
questions.explanation: Z = ρc, so Z rises with ρ.

questions.stem: If propagation speed increases while density remains constant, acoustic impedance will:
questions.explanation: Z = ρc, so Z rises with c.

questions.stem: A larger difference between Z1 and Z2 produces:
questions.explanation: Larger mismatch gives more reflection and less transmission.

questions.stem: When Z1 = Z2, which outcome occurs at perpendicular incidence?
questions.explanation: Equal impedances produce no reflection; everything is transmitted.

questions.stem: The intensity reflection coefficient represents the:
options: Speed of sound at an interface
questions.explanation: IRC is the fraction of incident intensity that is reflected.

questions.stem: Which formula calculates IRC when incident and reflected intensities are known?
questions.explanation: IRC = Ir/Ii.

questions.stem: Which formula calculates IRC from acoustic impedances at perpendicular incidence?
questions.explanation: Difference over sum, then squared.

questions.stem: An IRC of 0 indicates:
questions.explanation: IRC = 0 means no reflected intensity.

questions.stem: An IRC of 1 represents:
questions.explanation: IRC = 1 means all incident intensity is reflected.

questions.stem: Which formula describes the relationship between IRC and ITC?
questions.explanation: IRC + ITC = 1.

questions.stem: If the IRC at an interface is 0.25, what is the ITC?
Which combination represents complete transmission?
questions.explanation: No reflection and all transmitted.

questions.stem: Why is coupling gel placed between the transducer and the skin?
options: To increase reflection at the skin surface
To increase the propagation speed in tissue
To eliminate air and improve sound transmission
questions.explanation: Gel removes the air layer and improves transmission.

questions.stem: At an interface, the incident intensity is equal to:
questions.explanation: Ii = Ir + It (conservation of energy).

questions.stem: If the incident intensity is 10 mW/cm² and the reflected intensity is 2 mW/cm², what is the transmitted intensity?
questions.explanation: It = 10 − 2 = 8 mW/cm².

questions.stem: If the incident intensity is 20 mW/cm² and the reflected intensity is 5 mW/cm², what is the IRC?
If the IRC is 0.15, what percentage of the incident intensity is transmitted?
At perpendicular incidence, what occurs when the acoustic impedances of two media are equal?
questions.explanation: The impedance difference is zero, so there is no reflected echo and It = Ii.

questions.stem: Which interface would be expected to produce the greatest reflection?
questions.explanation: Soft tissue–air has a very large impedance mismatch.

questions.stem: A smooth tissue boundary appears poorly defined despite adequate gain. Which action should the sonographer try first?
questions.explanation: Changing the angle can redirect a specular reflection back toward the transducer.

questions.stem: Which structure is most likely to behave as a specular reflector?
questions.explanation: The diaphragm is a large, smooth boundary.

questions.stem: A beam strikes an interface at 90° to the interface surface. What is the angle of incidence measured from the normal?
questions.explanation: A beam perpendicular to the interface lies along the normal (0°).

questions.stem: Why may a smooth interface appear less echogenic at oblique incidence?
options: The reflected beam may miss the transducer
questions.explanation: Reflected sound travels away at an angle and may not return to the transducer.

questions.stem: Which factor determines whether the transmitted beam changes direction at an oblique interface?
questions.explanation: Refraction requires a propagation-speed difference (and oblique incidence).

questions.stem: If the intensity reflection coefficient increases, the intensity transmission coefficient will:
questions.explanation: IRC + ITC = 1.

questions.stem: Which intensity relationship represents complete reflection?
questions.explanation: All incident intensity is reflected, none transmitted.

questions.stem: Which intensity relationship represents complete transmission?
questions.explanation: IRC = 0 and ITC = 1.

questions.stem: What is the primary consequence of scanning without coupling gel?
options: Nearly complete reflection at the air–skin interface
Increased propagation speed in soft tissue
questions.explanation: The air layer causes a huge impedance mismatch and nearly total reflection. ---

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a possible interaction of ultrasound with tissue?
questions.explanation: Sound can be reflected, transmitted, absorbed, scattered or refracted. Tissue does not amplify it.

questions.stem: Conversion of ultrasound energy into heat within tissue is called:
questions.explanation: Absorption converts sound energy to heat and reduces intensity with depth.

questions.stem: Ultrasound that passes through a tissue without changing direction is best described as:
questions.explanation: Transmission carries energy deeper without a change in direction.

questions.stem: Bending of the transmitted wave at a boundary between media with different propagation speeds is called:
questions.explanation: Refraction is a change in direction of the transmitted beam at an oblique interface.

questions.stem: Which statement about image formation is correct?
options: Transmitted sound alone forms the image
Without returning echoes, no pulse-echo image can be formed
Echoes are not required to produce grayscale
questions.explanation: Pulse-echo imaging depends entirely on echoes returning to the transducer.

questions.stem: In a grayscale image, echo strength determines the:
questions.explanation: Stronger echoes are displayed brighter; position is determined by arrival time.

questions.stem: The boundary where the liver meets the diaphragm is an example of:
questions.explanation: An interface is where two media with different properties meet.

questions.stem: If no absorption occurs, the reflected plus transmitted intensities at a boundary equal:
questions.explanation: Reflection % + transmission % = 100% of the incident intensity.

questions.stem: The principle that reflected plus transmitted energy must equal incident energy is an example of:
questions.explanation: Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only redistributed.

questions.stem: Echoes from an interface with a large impedance mismatch will appear:
questions.explanation: A large mismatch gives high IRC, strong reflection and a bright echo.

questions.stem: Which of the following does NOT significantly determine the amount of reflection at an interface?
options: Angle and width of the tissue boundary
questions.explanation: Reflection depends on incidence angle, impedance mismatch, and boundary width and angle. PRF is a system setting.

questions.stem: Reflection is best described as:
options: A change in wave direction at a boundary that returns some energy toward the source
Complete conversion of sound to heat
A decrease in wavelength to zero
questions.explanation: Reflection sends part of the incident energy back into the first medium.

questions.stem: The endocardial border is visible against the blood pool even though blood and myocardium have similar impedances. The echo at this boundary is:
options: Absent, because the impedances are equal
Stronger than at an air–tissue boundary
A weak reflection from a small impedance difference
questions.explanation: A small impedance difference gives a small IRC. Most sound is transmitted, but the smooth endocardium still returns a weak specular echo.

questions.stem: The granular texture of the liver parenchyma on ultrasound is produced mainly by:
questions.explanation: Small structures within tissue scatter sound in many directions, producing a diffuse echo pattern.

questions.stem: An interface reflects 30% of the incident intensity and none is absorbed. The remaining 70% is:
questions.explanation: With no absorption, whatever is not reflected is transmitted (ITC = 0.70).

questions.stem: Specular reflection occurs when the reflector is:
options: Large and smooth relative to the wavelength
questions.explanation: Boundary much larger than the wavelength produces mirror-like reflection.

questions.stem: The word "specular" refers to:
questions.explanation: Specular reflection behaves like light off a flat mirror.

questions.stem: Which structure is the best example of a specular reflector?
questions.explanation: The pericardium is a thin, smooth, large layer that produces bright, angle-dependent echoes.

questions.stem: Reflection from reflectors much smaller than the wavelength is called:
questions.explanation: Boundary << wavelength gives Rayleigh scattering and back scatter.

questions.stem: A boundary roughly similar in size to the wavelength produces mainly:
questions.explanation: Boundary \~ wavelength gives diffuse reflection.

questions.stem: Which description best fits diffuse reflection (scattering)?
options: Sound redirected in many directions from small or irregular reflectors
questions.explanation: Scattering disperses the wave over a wide range of directions.

questions.stem: Which type of reflection is most dependent on the angle of the beam?
questions.explanation: Specular reflection is highly angle dependent.

questions.stem: When the beam is perpendicular to a smooth endocardial surface, the border appears:
questions.explanation: The endocardium gives crisp specular reflections when the beam is perpendicular.

questions.stem: Red blood cells are much smaller than the ultrasound wavelength. They produce weak echoes mainly through:
questions.explanation: Very small reflectors produce Rayleigh scattering.

questions.stem: Compared with specular echoes, scattered echoes are generally:
questions.explanation: Scattering spreads energy over many angles, so each echo is weaker but less dependent on beam angle.

questions.stem: Which pairing of reflector and reflection type is correct?
options: Red blood cell and specular reflection
questions.explanation: Smooth vessel walls produce specular reflection.

questions.stem: A boundary that is much larger than the wavelength produces:
questions.explanation: Boundary >> wavelength gives specular reflection.

questions.stem: A large, smooth boundary struck at an oblique angle will:
options: Return most of its echo to the transducer
Reflect sound equally in all directions
Direct its reflected echo away from the transducer
questions.explanation: Angle of reflection equals angle of incidence, so the echo leaves obliquely and may miss the transducer.

questions.stem: A smooth 10 mm vessel wall is insonated with a pulse whose wavelength is about 0.5 mm. The reflection is mainly:
questions.explanation: The boundary is much larger than the wavelength.

questions.stem: The speckle texture seen in solid organs is mainly produced by:
questions.explanation: Small structures and irregularities within tissue scatter sound diffusely.

questions.stem: The normal is:
options: A line parallel to the interface
An imaginary line perpendicular to the interface at the point of incidence
questions.explanation: The normal is the reference line from which all angles are measured.

questions.stem: The angles of incidence, reflection and transmission are all measured from:
questions.explanation: Angles are measured from the normal, not from the boundary surface.

questions.stem: A beam strikes an interface at 30° to the interface surface. What is the angle of incidence?
questions.explanation: The normal is 90° from the surface, so the incidence angle is 90° − 30° = 60°.

questions.stem: The angle of incidence is 25°. The angle of reflection is:
questions.explanation: Angle of reflection = angle of incidence.

questions.stem: A beam has an incidence angle of 40°. What is the angle between the incident beam and the reflected beam?
questions.explanation: The two beams lie 40° on either side of the normal: 40° + 40° = 80°.

questions.stem: The transmission angle depends on:
options: The incidence angle and the propagation speeds of the two media
questions.explanation: Transmission angle is governed by the incidence angle and the speed difference.

questions.stem: Which angle is always equal to the angle of incidence?
questions.explanation: Incidence angle always equals reflection angle.

questions.stem: Perpendicular incidence is also called:
questions.explanation: Perpendicular and normal incidence are the same.

questions.stem: Tissue boundaries oriented \_\_\_\_ to the beam act as excellent reflectors.
questions.explanation: Perpendicular boundaries return echoes straight back.

questions.stem: Tissue boundaries that are parallel to the beam path act as:
questions.explanation: The beam barely meets the surface, so little echo returns.

questions.stem: Compared with oblique incidence, perpendicular incidence on a smooth interface generally produces:
questions.explanation: Perpendicular incidence returns the echo along the incident path.

questions.stem: A ball dropped straight down onto the floor bounces straight back up. This is an analogy for:
questions.explanation: The reflected path retraces the incident path.

questions.stem: Which angle of incidence would be expected to return the weakest echo to the transducer from a smooth interface?
questions.explanation: The more oblique the incidence, the further the reflected beam is directed from the transducer.

questions.stem: In the lecture diagram, the angle between the incident beam and the normal is labelled:
questions.explanation: θi = incidence, θr = reflection, θt = transmission.

questions.stem: If two media have identical propagation speeds, the transmitted beam at an oblique interface:
options: Continues at an angle equal to the incidence angle
Travels at twice the incidence angle
questions.explanation: No speed difference means no refraction, so the beam does not bend.

questions.stem: A normal, smooth structure appears dim from one transducer position. The most appropriate interpretation is:
options: It may be an angle-related imaging problem
questions.explanation: A dim structure does not necessarily mean abnormality. Reflected sound may simply be directed away.

questions.stem: Which of the following can improve beam alignment with a smooth interface?
options: Angling, rocking, sliding or repositioning the transducer
questions.explanation: The goal is to make the beam as perpendicular to the structure as possible.

questions.stem: In an apical four-chamber view, the interventricular septum is nearly parallel to the beam. Its echoes will most likely be:
questions.explanation: Reflections from a near-parallel surface are directed away from the transducer.

questions.stem: In the parasternal long-axis view, the beam crosses the interventricular septum nearly perpendicularly. The septal borders typically appear:
questions.explanation: Near-perpendicular incidence gives strong specular reflection.

questions.stem: A healthy patient's lateral LV wall is poorly seen in an apical view. The most likely physical explanation is:
options: Z1 equals Z2 at the endocardium
Absorption of sound by coupling gel
Echoes from the near-parallel endocardial surface are reflected away from the transducer
An IRC of 1 at the endocardium
questions.explanation: Oblique or near-parallel incidence directs specular echoes away from the transducer.

questions.stem: Acoustic impedance represents the resistance a medium offers to:
questions.explanation: Impedance is the resistance a tissue provides to sound transmission, set by density and propagation speed.

questions.stem: Which of the following has the highest acoustic impedance?
questions.explanation: Bone is about 6.7 MRayl. Water is about 1.5, lung about 0.26 and air about 0.0004.

questions.stem: Which of the following has the lowest acoustic impedance?
questions.explanation: Air is about 0.0004 MRayl, far lower than lung (0.26) or soft tissue.

questions.stem: A medium has a density of 1000 kg/m³ and a propagation speed of 1500 m/s. Its acoustic impedance is:
A medium has a density of 1200 kg/m³ and a propagation speed of 1500 m/s. Its acoustic impedance is:
Bone has a high acoustic impedance mainly because of its:
options: High density and high propagation speed
questions.explanation: Bone has both high density (about 1500 kg/m³) and high speed (about 4080 m/s), so their product is large.

questions.stem: Air has a very low acoustic impedance because it has:
options: Very low density and low propagation speed
questions.explanation: Air is about 1.2 kg/m³ with a speed of about 330 m/s.

questions.stem: Density doubles while propagation speed stays constant. Acoustic impedance:
questions.explanation: Z = ρc, so Z is directly proportional to density.

questions.stem: Both density and propagation speed double. Acoustic impedance:
One MRayl is equal to:
questions.explanation: "M" denotes mega (10⁶).

questions.stem: Which interface has the largest impedance mismatch?
questions.explanation: Bone (about 6.7 MRayl) differs far more from soft tissue than the other pairs, which are all similar.

questions.stem: Which interface has the smallest impedance mismatch?
questions.explanation: Liver and spleen have nearly identical impedances (about 1.65 MRayl).

questions.stem: For reflection to occur at a perpendicular interface, the two media must have:
questions.explanation: A difference in impedance is required. Equal impedances give no reflection.

questions.stem: Acoustic impedance is NOT affected by:
questions.explanation: Impedance is a property of the medium (ρ × c) and does not depend on the transducer's frequency.

questions.stem: Acoustic impedance is calculated from density and propagation speed as their:
questions.explanation: Z = ρ × c.

questions.stem: Lung has a low acoustic impedance compared with soft tissue primarily because:
options: Its air content lowers both its density and its propagation speed
Its density is greater than blood
questions.explanation: Lung is about 400 kg/m³ with a speed of about 500 m/s, giving Z of about 0.26 MRayl.

questions.stem: Which two substances produce very bright echoes because of a large impedance mismatch with soft tissue?
questions.explanation: Air (very low Z) and bone (very high Z) are strong reflectors against soft tissue.

questions.stem: A PZT crystal (about 38 MRayl) placed directly on skin (soft tissue about 1.6–2 MRayl) would transmit poorly. This is why transducers include a:
questions.explanation: A matching layer of intermediate impedance reduces the mismatch and improves transmission.

questions.stem: A matching layer on a transducer has an impedance between that of the PZT and tissue. It:
options: Improves transmission by reducing the mismatch
questions.explanation: The matching layer steps the impedance down so more sound enters the body.

questions.stem: What matters most at an interface is:
options: The difference in impedance between the two media
The impedance of the first medium alone
The density of the second medium alone
The propagation speed of the first medium alone
questions.explanation: Reflection depends on the impedance mismatch between the two media, not on either value alone.

questions.stem: Z1 = 1.0 MRayl and Z2 = 3.0 MRayl. What is the IRC?
Z1 = 1.0 MRayl and Z2 = 3.0 MRayl. What is the ITC?
Z1 = 2 MRayl and Z2 = 6 MRayl. What percentage of the incident intensity is reflected?
Two media each have an impedance of 1.6 MRayl. The IRC is:
questions.explanation: The difference is zero, so there is no reflection. ITC = 1.

questions.stem: Z1 = 1 MRayl and Z2 = 9 MRayl. What is the IRC?
questions.explanation: IRC = (8/10)² = 0.64. The value 0.80 results from forgetting to square.

questions.stem: Z1 = 4 MRayl and Z2 = 6 MRayl. What percentage of the incident intensity is reflected?
Z1 = 2 MRayl and Z2 = 8 MRayl. What percentage of the incident intensity is transmitted?
Sound travels from a medium with Z1 = 3 MRayl into one with Z2 = 1 MRayl. What is the IRC?
questions.explanation: IRC = (−2/4)² = 0.25. Squaring removes the sign, so the result is the same as for 1 → 3 MRayl.

questions.stem: Ii = 50 mW/cm² and Ir = 5 mW/cm². What is the IRC?
Ii = 40 mW/cm² and the IRC is 0.20. What is the reflected intensity?
questions.explanation: Ir = IRC × Ii = 0.20 × 40 = 8 mW/cm².

questions.stem: Ii = 40 mW/cm² and the IRC is 0.20. What is the transmitted intensity?
Ii = 100 mW/cm² and It = 64 mW/cm². What is the IRC?
The ITC at an interface is 0.90. What percentage of the incident intensity is reflected?
An interface reflects 99% of the incident intensity. The ITC is:
The units of the intensity reflection coefficient are:
questions.explanation: IRC is a ratio of two intensities, so it has no units. The same is true of ITC.

questions.stem: For an air (0.0004 MRayl) to soft tissue (about 1.63 MRayl) interface, the IRC is approximately:
The impedance of water is 1.48 MRayl and liver is 1.65 MRayl. The IRC at this interface is approximately:
questions.explanation: IRC = (0.17/3.13)², which is about 0.003 (0.3%). Almost all the sound is transmitted.

questions.stem: Heart muscle (1.74 MRayl) lies against lung (0.26 MRayl). The percentage of intensity reflected is approximately:
questions.explanation: IRC = (−1.48/2.00)² = 0.5476, about 55% reflected. About 45% is transmitted.

questions.stem: A PZT crystal (38 MRayl) contacts tissue (1.63 MRayl) with no matching layer. The percentage of sound reflected is approximately:
questions.explanation: IRC = (36.37/39.63)², about 0.84. Most of the sound is reflected back into the crystal, so poor transmission results.

questions.stem: Which pair of impedances (in MRayl) produces an IRC of 0.25?
questions.explanation: (3 − 1)/(3 + 1) = 0.5 and 0.5² = 0.25. The other pairs give about 0.11, 0.36 and 0.04.

questions.stem: Which interface would produce the greatest IRC?
questions.explanation: IRC is about 0.54 for C, compared with about 0.03 for B and well under 0.01 for A and D.

questions.stem: As the impedance mismatch at an interface increases, the IRC \_\_\_\_ and the ITC \_\_\_\_.
options: Stays the same; stays the same
questions.explanation: More mismatch gives more reflection and less transmission.

questions.stem: Which statement is true for an interface with an IRC of 0.04?
options: It has a very large impedance mismatch
questions.explanation: ITC = 1 − 0.04 = 0.96. A small IRC means a small mismatch.

questions.stem: Z1 = 1.5 MRayl and Z2 = 1.7 MRayl. The IRC is approximately:
questions.explanation: IRC = (0.2/3.2)², about 0.004 (0.4%). Nearly all the sound is transmitted.

questions.stem: At perpendicular incidence, the IRC calculated from impedances depends on:
questions.explanation: IRC = \[(Z2 − Z1)/(Z2 + Z1)\]² uses both impedances.

questions.stem: Ii = 2 mW/cm² and It = 0.5 mW/cm². What is the ITC?
The ITC at an interface is 0.25. What is the IRC?
questions.explanation: IRC = 1 − ITC = 0.75.

questions.stem: If no sound is transmitted at an interface, the IRC is:
questions.explanation: All the incident intensity is reflected (Ir = Ii).

questions.stem: Ii = 12 mW/cm² and the ITC is 0.90. What is the reflected intensity?
questions.explanation: IRC = 0.10, so Ir = 0.10 × 12 = 1.2 mW/cm². (10.8 is the transmitted intensity.)

questions.stem: For any interface with no absorption, IRC + ITC equals:
questions.explanation: All incident sound is either reflected or transmitted, so IRC + ITC = 1 (100%).

questions.stem: The air–skin interface produces nearly total reflection because:
options: Air has a very high density
Air has a very high propagation speed
The impedance of air is far lower than that of skin
questions.explanation: A huge impedance mismatch (0.0004 vs about 1.6 MRayl) gives an IRC near 1.
tags: Coupling Gel and Clinical Echocardiography Applications

questions.stem: Coupling gel improves imaging by:
options: Eliminating the air layer and reducing the impedance mismatch
Increasing the propagation speed in tissue
questions.explanation: Gel provides a good sound path from transducer to skin and improves transmission.
tags: Coupling Gel and Clinical Echocardiography Applications

questions.stem: Without gel, the IRC at the transducer–air–skin interface is approximately:
questions.explanation: Almost all the sound (about 99.9%) is reflected.
tags: Coupling Gel and Clinical Echocardiography Applications

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a purpose of coupling gel?
options: To provide a good sound path
To increase reflection at the skin surface
To improve transmission into the body
questions.explanation: The purpose of gel is to improve transmission, not to increase reflection.
tags: Coupling Gel and Clinical Echocardiography Applications

questions.stem: Lung tissue overlying the heart degrades the echo image because:
options: Air-filled lung forms a large impedance mismatch with soft tissue and reflects most of the sound
Lung has a higher impedance than bone
Lung has the same impedance as soft tissue
questions.explanation: Lung impedance (about 0.26 MRayl) is far below that of soft tissue, so most of the sound is reflected.
tags: Coupling Gel and Clinical Echocardiography Applications

questions.stem: During an echo, part of the image near the transducer face suddenly drops out. The gel under the transducer has dried in that area. The best first action is to:
options: Reapply gel to eliminate the air gap
questions.explanation: Air under the transducer reflects almost all of the sound. Restoring gel restores transmission.
tags: Coupling Gel and Clinical Echocardiography Applications

questions.stem: A pocket of air trapped between the transducer and skin will most likely cause:
options: Loss of image information beneath it because most sound is reflected
questions.explanation: The air–skin mismatch reflects nearly all the incident sound.
tags: Coupling Gel and Clinical Echocardiography Applications

questions.stem: Ribs and sternum limit transthoracic echo windows because:
options: Bone creates a large impedance mismatch, so most sound is reflected and little is transmitted
Bone has the same impedance as soft tissue
questions.explanation: Bone (about 6.7 MRayl) differs greatly from soft tissue.
tags: Coupling Gel and Clinical Echocardiography Applications

questions.stem: Which of the following typically produces the brightest echoes in an echo exam because of a large impedance mismatch?
questions.explanation: Calcium and prosthetic material differ greatly in impedance from soft tissue.
tags: Coupling Gel and Clinical Echocardiography Applications

questions.stem: Distal to a mechanical prosthetic valve, the image often shows weak or absent echoes. This is because:
options: Most of the sound is reflected at the high-impedance prosthesis, so little is transmitted distally
questions.explanation: A very large mismatch produces strong reflection and little transmission.
tags: Coupling Gel and Clinical Echocardiography Applications

questions.stem: Blood in a cardiac chamber normally appears dark (anechoic) mainly because:
options: It has an impedance of zero
It has a very high propagation speed
Its scatterers are much smaller than the wavelength and give only very weak echoes
questions.explanation: Red blood cells produce weak Rayleigh scattering, so little echo returns.
tags: Coupling Gel and Clinical Echocardiography Applications

questions.stem: Which beam–interface relationship gives the best endocardial border definition?
questions.explanation: Specular reflection is strongest at perpendicular incidence.
tags: Coupling Gel and Clinical Echocardiography Applications

questions.stem: The septum appears poorly defined because it is nearly parallel to the beam. The sonographer should:
options: Use a window that places the beam more perpendicular to the septum
questions.explanation: Changing the angle or window restores perpendicular incidence.
tags: Coupling Gel and Clinical Echocardiography Applications

questions.stem: In which view is the interventricular septum typically most nearly parallel to the ultrasound beam?
questions.explanation: In the apical four-chamber view the beam runs along the long axis of the septum, so echo dropout can occur.
tags: Coupling Gel and Clinical Echocardiography Applications

questions.stem: The IRC at an interface is 0.003. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
options: The interface will be very bright
Most sound is transmitted and the interface returns only a weak echo
questions.explanation: An IRC of 0.003 means 0.3% is reflected and 99.7% is transmitted.
tags: Coupling Gel and Clinical Echocardiography Applications

questions.stem: Using Z = 1.63 MRayl for soft tissue and 6.7 MRayl for bone, the IRC at a soft tissue–bone interface is approximately:
questions.explanation: (6.7 − 1.63)/(6.7 + 1.63) = 0.61 and 0.61² is about 0.37, so about 37% is reflected.
tags: Coupling Gel and Clinical Echocardiography Applications

questions.stem: Using Z = 1.63 MRayl for soft tissue and 0.26 MRayl for lung, the percentage of sound transmitted is approximately:
tags: Coupling Gel and Clinical Echocardiography Applications

questions.stem: Liver (1.66 MRayl) lies next to blood (1.62 MRayl). The percentage of sound transmitted is approximately:
questions.explanation: IRC = (0.04/3.28)², which is about 0.00015. The impedances are almost equal.
tags: Coupling Gel and Clinical Echocardiography Applications

questions.stem: The reflection at a fat (1.35 MRayl) to muscle (1.70 MRayl) interface is approximately:
tags: Coupling Gel and Clinical Echocardiography Applications

questions.stem: With gel eliminating the air gap, the IRC at the transducer–gel–skin path is approximately:
questions.explanation: Gel has an impedance close to that of soft tissue, so the mismatch is minimal and nearly all sound is transmitted.
tags: Coupling Gel and Clinical Echocardiography Applications

questions.stem: Which term describes a structure that appears black with no internal echoes?
questions.explanation: Anechoic structures (fluid-filled) return no echoes.

questions.stem: Bone, fat and calcification typically appear:
questions.explanation: They return strong echoes and appear bright (white).

questions.stem: A structure that has the same brightness as its surroundings is described as:
questions.explanation: Isoechoic tissue blends in with its surroundings.

questions.stem: Solid tumours, lymph nodes and oedema typically appear dark gray with low-level echoes. This is termed:
questions.explanation: Hypoechoic means lower echo strength than the reference tissue.

questions.stem: A pericardial effusion appears:
questions.explanation: Simple fluid returns no echoes, so it appears black.

questions.stem: Which term describes tissue that is brighter than a reference tissue but not as bright as bone or calcification?
questions.explanation: Echogenic tissue produces noticeable echoes. Valve leaflets and the pericardium are examples.

questions.stem: Which term and echo strength are correctly paired?
questions.explanation: Anechoic = none, hypoechoic = low, isoechoic = equal, hyperechoic = high.

questions.stem: Bone and calcification appear hyperechoic mainly because:
options: They have a large impedance mismatch with surrounding soft tissue
Their propagation speed equals that of soft tissue
They have a very low density
questions.explanation: A large mismatch produces a high IRC and strong, bright echoes.

questions.stem: Valve leaflets and the pericardium are typically described as:
questions.explanation: They return noticeable echoes and are brighter than the surrounding tissue.

questions.stem: An isoechoic lesion within the liver is difficult to detect because:
options: Its echo brightness is similar to that of the surrounding tissue
It is much brighter than the liver
questions.explanation: Similar echogenicity means little contrast with the surrounding tissue.

questions.stem: Refraction requires:
options: Perpendicular incidence and equal propagation speeds
Oblique incidence and equal propagation speeds
Oblique incidence and different propagation speeds
questions.explanation: A change in the transmitted direction needs both an oblique angle and a speed difference.

questions.stem: Acoustic impedance differences determine \_\_\_\_, while propagation speed differences determine \_\_\_\_.
options: How much sound is reflected and transmitted; the direction of the transmitted beam
The direction of the reflected beam; the amount transmitted
questions.explanation: Impedance controls the proportion reflected and transmitted. Speed controls refraction.

questions.stem: At perpendicular incidence, a transmitted beam crossing into a medium with a different propagation speed:
questions.explanation: The beam travels along the normal, so no bending occurs.

questions.stem: Which of the following can occur at oblique incidence but NOT at perpendicular incidence?
questions.explanation: Refraction needs an oblique angle.

questions.stem: At an interface Ir is approximately equal to Ii. Which statement is true?
options: There is a very large impedance mismatch and ITC is approximately 0
The beam is at 90° to the normal
questions.explanation: Nearly all the incident intensity is reflected, so very little is transmitted.

questions.stem: Which combination produces the brightest echo from a smooth interface?
questions.explanation: The strongest returning echoes need both an impedance difference and perpendicular incidence.

questions.stem: Which condition produces NO reflection at perpendicular incidence?
options: Equal impedances, even if the densities and speeds differ
questions.explanation: Only Z1 = Z2 gives IRC = 0.

questions.stem: Two media have the same density but different propagation speeds. At perpendicular incidence:
options: No reflection occurs because the densities are equal
Reflection occurs because the impedances differ
No reflection occurs because the frequencies are equal
Reflection occurs only at oblique incidence
questions.explanation: Z = ρc, so different speeds mean different impedances.

questions.stem: The lung hampers imaging of structures deep to it because:
options: Lung has a very high impedance
Air in the lung forms a large mismatch with soft tissue and reflects nearly all the sound
Lung refracts the beam toward the normal
questions.explanation: Air is an extreme impedance mismatch with soft tissue.

questions.stem: 25% of the incident intensity is reflected at the first interface. The transmitted portion meets a second interface that reflects 20% of the intensity reaching it. What fraction of the original incident intensity is reflected from the second interface? (Ignore attenuation.)
questions.explanation: Transmitted at the first interface = 0.75. Reflected at the second = 0.20 × 0.75 = 0.15.

questions.stem: Ii = 100 mW/cm². The first interface has an IRC of 0.10 and the second interface has an ITC of 0.80. What intensity is transmitted beyond the second interface? (Ignore attenuation.)
questions.explanation: After the first interface: 100 × 0.90 = 90. After the second: 90 × 0.80 = 72 mW/cm².

questions.stem: Which statement is NOT true of specular reflection?
options: It obeys angle of reflection = angle of incidence
It is independent of the beam angle
It occurs at large, smooth boundaries
questions.explanation: Specular reflection is highly angle dependent.

questions.stem: At which angle of incidence will the echo from a smooth interface return directly to the transducer?
questions.explanation: Only at 0° does the reflected beam retrace the incident path.

questions.stem: A smooth interface is struck at 10° from the normal. The reflected beam leaves:
options: At 10° from the normal on the opposite side, away from the incident path
At 20° from the normal on the same side
questions.explanation: Angle of reflection = angle of incidence, on the opposite side of the normal.

questions.stem: Which action would NOT improve visualization of a poorly seen smooth boundary?
questions.explanation: PRF does not change the incidence angle. Angling, rocking, sliding or repositioning does.

questions.stem: The IRC at soft tissue–air is about 1 and at soft tissue–bone about 0.37. Which conclusion is most accurate?
questions.explanation: Air has the larger impedance mismatch with soft tissue, so its IRC is higher.

questions.stem: Without coupling gel, approximately what percentage of the incident intensity enters the tissue?
questions.explanation: About 99.9% is reflected, so only about 0.1% is transmitted.

questions.stem: Which is the best clinical example of complete (or nearly complete) reflection?
questions.explanation: IRC is approximately 1 and ITC is approximately 0.

questions.stem: Materials A and B each have Z = 1.4 MRayl and material C has Z = 6.0 MRayl. Which interface produces no reflection at perpendicular incidence?
questions.explanation: Equal impedances mean IRC = 0.

questions.stem: Z2 is twice Z1. What is the IRC?
The image behind a densely calcified mitral annulus is dark. The best explanation is:
options: Little sound reaches deeper structures because most is reflected at the interface
questions.explanation: A very large mismatch reflects most of the sound, so little is transmitted beyond it.

questions.stem: The statement "no reflection, no image" means that:
options: Pulse-echo imaging depends entirely on reflection
Imaging is based on transmission alone
questions.explanation: Without returning echoes, no pulse-echo image can be formed.

questions.stem: The strongest returning echoes from a smooth interface occur when:
options: There is an impedance difference and the beam is parallel to the interface
There is an impedance difference and the beam is perpendicular to the interface
The impedances are equal and the beam is perpendicular
The impedances are equal and the beam is oblique
questions.explanation: Both an impedance difference and perpendicular incidence are required.

questions.stem: The amount of reflection is determined primarily by \_\_\_\_, and the direction of reflection by \_\_\_\_.
questions.explanation: Mismatch sets the strength. Incidence angle sets the direction.

questions.stem: Which list places these interfaces in order of INCREASING IRC? (Fat–muscle ≈ 0.013; liver–spleen ≈ 0; soft tissue–bone ≈ 0.37; soft tissue–air ≈ 0.999)
options: Soft tissue–air, soft tissue–bone, fat–muscle, liver–spleen
Soft tissue–bone, fat–muscle, liver–spleen, soft tissue–air
Fat–muscle, liver–spleen, soft tissue–air, soft tissue–bone
Liver–spleen, fat–muscle, soft tissue–bone, soft tissue–air
questions.explanation: The smaller the impedance mismatch, the lower the IRC. ---
